doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

chapter: Maynard, Bobby Shew and the trumpet
title: Breathing, Bobby Shew and playing efficiently
summary: Bergeron on Maynard's breathing, Bobby Shew's teaching, modern equipment, and being stronger at 62 than at 30.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Wasn’t a big part of his success as a trumpet player having something to do with his breathing?

Yeah. I mean he talked about, you know, the yoga breath and things he learned in India, and which Bobby Shew teaches as well. And Bobby Shew kind of learned these things from him. So I would say yes. But Maynard was doing that long before he learned how to do that. I mean Maynard was playing unbelievably efficient way before he learned about Eastern philosophy and different kinds of breathing. I mean I think it enhanced his playing later and made him even more efficient. And Bobby Shew, you know, teaches a thing called the wedge breath, which is all based on these things that Maynard did, which I do. Like I said I just took another lesson with Bobby recently. I mean I think, just let it © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

be known, I think Bobby Shew is the greatest brass educator in a hundred years. Because, you know, us trumpet players and brass players, we kind of have our heads stuck in the sand of tradition and that’s Bobby’s line. You’ve got your head stuck in the sand of tradition. When you’re looking at these books and concepts from over a hundred years ago, you know, things around the turn of the century, you know of the 1900s, of how we played the trumpet or the cornet at the time. And we’re still trying to apply those to modern day musicians. Now are those things valid? Of course. There’s a lot of great information in the foundation of where those players come from. But we’ve also learned a few things over the years. I mean, you know, we know that the computer is going to do better math than an abacus you know. So we kind of need to move on and kind of learn from technology a little bit. You know we’ve made some better trumpets, even though a lot of people say, “Oh the old horns are better.” They’re not better. There was a lot of old horns that were great. A lot of them sucked because they were so inconsistent. We’ve learned a lot of stuff. You know fine tooling machining is going to be better than some wiggly lathe they used in the 30s, you know, to cut a piece of metal. Let’s face it. You know so they can say that all they want. And the metal was better — I don’t buy any of it. But, so we’ve learned a few things. And we’ve learned a few things about efficiency and how to play the trumpet more efficiently, and maybe the mouthpiece being able to help a little bit and where there’s that school of thought that, oh you just play the mouthpiece that came with the horn and you work hard. Or you play a 7C and you just work hard and you do everything on that mouthpiece. Well you can do that and your career is probably going to be over by the time you’re 55 years old because you’ve been working so hard that your body shuts down. And a lot of players from yesteryear, you know, from the 40s that played bigger mouthpieces than kind of we do now, all their careers were — very few of them were playing into their 80s of any of them. Whereas now we have Doc Severinsen at 93 years old who can still hit a high G. And we have Bobby Shew who is going to be 80 years old very soon, and he can still play a double high C better than most 30 year olds. So we’ve learned a few things about how to be more efficient and how to use the right equipment for the job. And Bobby is a big proponent of that, of getting players to be smart about their equipment. And I learned that way too late in life. But here I’m going to be 63 years old in a few weeks and I’m stronger. And even recovering from cancer and losing 50 pounds and I’m still coming back, I’m stronger right now at this moment than I was when I was 30, as a player. I could bury a 30-year-old Wayne Bergeron. I could bury him, endurance-wise and everything. So I did something right along the way and I think grasping something that Bobby Shew said along the way is why I can do that. And a few other people too that I’ve learned from of course. © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
